newsitem.title: FRANCE: Germany may fail Maastricht - ex-Buba head Poehl.
newsitem.headline: Germany may fail Maastricht - ex-Buba head Poehl.

text.p: Germany looks unlikely to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on debt and deficits, posing a tough problem for the government on the road to European monetary union, former Bundesbank head Karl Otto Poehl said on Tuesday.

He told a conference that while his starting assumption was that monetary union would be launched on time in 1999, "it could still be possible that the whole excercise will be postponed or may even fail."
"What appears particularly worrying is the fact that Germany is far away from meeting the (Maastricht) target," he said.

He also said he found French calls for a political authority to act as a counterbalance to the future European Central Bank (ECB) "extremely worrying", saying an independent central bank had been a condition of German acceptance of monetary union.
Germany was likely to overshoot Maastricht treaty requirements limiting public deficits this year to three percent of gross domestic product and debt to 60 percent of GDP.
"It could happen that we meet these targets, but I don't think it's very likely. Without a considerable acceleration of economic growth, Germany will fail to meet the deficit criteria," he said.
Germany however was in the difficult situation of having told its European partners and its own people the Maastricht treaty must be interpreted strictly. "It's a little ugly."
"It's a political and psychological problem in Germany," he said, adding that the German public would lose all confidence in monetary union project if Maastricht criteria were fudged.
"I have no idea how the government will solve this very delicate problem," he said.
He also slammed France's insistence that the question of the euro's exchange rate is too important to be left to the judgement of unelected central bank governors.
It wants a special council to co-ordinate economic and exchange rate policy in the euro zone and says Europe should use the euro to fight any competitive devaluation in the dollar.
"The European Central Bank is the centrepiece, the cornerstone of Economic and Monetary Union," Poehl said.
"The fact that the highest French representatives, if I understood what I read, ask for control. That is something which puts the whole concept into question," he said.
Poehl, who left the Bundesbank in 1991 after nine years as president, and is now a director of private bank Sal Oppenheim, was involved in early talks on monetary union in the 1980s.

"As far as exchange rate policy is concerned, I think there is a misunderstanding," he said. During early talks, France wanted a clear exchange rate policy, while Germany had said this should be left to markets.
The compromise was that governments would decide on major changes to the exchange rate system -- for example a return to fixed exchange rates worldwide, he said.
"The day-to-day operation of the exchange rate system is the subject of the central bank, not the governments," he said.
Moreover, the Maastricht treaty prevented the ECB from taking instructions from politicians.
"The central bank is not allowed to accept instructions, neither from governments nor from parliaments, nor the councils of the central bank," he added.

Poehl, however, acknowledged a lack of democratic control on the ECB. "This institution will be very powerful. You can argue this is not very democratic, but as long as it is efficient, as long as it provides us with a strong and stable European currency, I would overlook that," he said. REUTER
